Before you start the project, make sure that you have completed all How-To and Practice Activities within the lesson, which will greatly help you with this project. In this project, you will use what you have learned so far to create a basic web page introducing: you! We would love to learn about your educational goals, including what degree or certificate you may be taking the course for. ## Project Prep If you're reading this, you have successfully accepted the assignment invitation and cloned it to your computer. (Good job!) > If you need a refresher on any steps related to Accepting invitations and cloning your repo, refer to the [How To: Clone and Open a Repo](https://springfield.coursearc.com/content/cis-public/git-github-and-vs-code/working-on-activities-and-assignments#How-To-Clone-and-Open-a-Repo) tutorial. 1. If you haven't done so already, clone the repo to your computer. 2. Open the repo within VS Code. You can open this `readme.md` file within VS Code to view the project directions there. > **TIP:** It is recommended that you view the `README.md` file in **Preview Mode** using **Split View**. You can use the Split View feature (under the **View** menu, **Editor Layout** options) in VS Code to display the `Readme.md` file on one side of VS Code and the files you need to edit on the other side. You can also open the `Readme.md` file in Preview mode by right clicking on the file and selecting the **Open Preview** option. 3. If there are files and folders present other than this `readme.md` file, take some time to familiarize yourself with the files within the repo so you know where they are located. This will help you when asked to use them within the project directions. > **TIP:** Before beginning any work on the project, read through all the steps to understand what you will be doing. ## Create A Basic Web Page 1. Create a new blank HTML5 document. If you are using VS Code, click the **New File** button in the Explorer pane next to the name of the assignment. 0. Save the file as **template.html**. The file will be saved in the default user directory for GitHub. For example, on a Windows computer it should be saved to c:/users/JohnSmith/github-classroom/sc-web101-in-v1/projectRepo. **NOTE** The file will be saved into the folder for the specific project repo you are working on. Do not save the file to a different folder. If you do that, the file will not sync to your GitHub account when you Sync and Commit your work. 0. Using the appropriate tags, create **the four basic HTML elements**. 0. Insert **a multi-line HTML comment** within the head element of the web page with the following information: Course, Section, and Lesson Number and fill in the information for your course and lesson. For example: > Course: WEB101
Section: 99999
Lesson: 3 0. Give the **page a title** of: {Your MEID} - Template. Replace the {Your MEID} with your actual MEID, like the following example: > XYZ9876543 - Template 0. **Save** your web page. **Sync** your file to GitHub and apply a **Commit** that says: `Created template with basic HTML elements`. If you need a refresher on how to Sync and Apply a commit, refer to [How to Apply a Commit and Sync your Files to GitHub](https://springfield.coursearc.com/content/cis-public/git-github-and-vs-code/working-on-activities-and-assignments) 0. Using the appropriate tags, add the following content to your web page: - Create a **first-level heading** with the following text: Basic Template - Create a **paragraph** under this heading with dummy text (see Working with Paragraphs) as the text within the paragraph. - Create a **second-level heading** with your first and last name as the text. - **Add at least one paragraph** under this second-level heading with a brief intro about yourself so your instructor can get to know you a bit more. You can include details about your educational goals, what you hope to get out of the course, etc. - Create **another paragraph** after your bio paragraph(s) with general contact information with each contact method **on a separate line** within a single paragraph. Include: - The text "Phone:" along with a fake phone number. - The text "Email:" along with your student email address. 0. Create **another paragraph** for the page copyright info. For the text use the following format: > Copyright {YEAR} by {Your Full Name} 0. **Save** your web page. **Sync** your file to GitHub and apply a **Commit** that says: `Added Content`.
## Example Project This is an example of what the project should look like before you submit your project. ![Screenshot of Index.html page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sc-web101-in-v1/CourseResources/main/L3-example1.png)

This is done by submitting the Repo URL to the assignment in SpringLearn. > **TIP:** If you need a refresher on how to submit your work, view: [Submitting Assignments & Viewing Feedback](https://springfield.coursearc.com/content/cis-public/git-github-and-vs-code/submitting-assignments-and-viewing-feedback). 1. Homepage: Welcome to the Helping the Homeless website, here you can find information on some of the issues that the less fortunate in our communities face daily, and on the solutions page where we give some ideas on how you as an individual can help, as well as solutions that can be done on a more institutional level. Also consider looking to Show Your Support, where you can pledge your support as well as receive periodic updates on this issue, such as updated official stats or policies being pushed by local and federal governments. If there is one thing we hope visitors can take away from this site, it is to remember that homeless individuals are also human and deserve care and support. Policy Page: Purpose Statement- This website is dedicated to educating visitors about the issues facing our less fortunate in our communities, and not only the potential solutions our governments can take, but also what you as an individual can do to help as well. Accessibility Statement-We are dedicated to keeping this website accessible for all users viewing this with any kind of device. Issues Page: To help people who are homeless, it’s important to know just what kinds of challenges they face in their lives. Of course, it’s important to remember that the homeless population is not a homogenous group with identical experiences, they are all unique individuals, some with their own unique challenges in their lives. However, listed below are some common ones. Malnutrition, Stress, exposure to the elements, violence, unsanitary living conditions, limited access to healthcare, increased risk of disease. (National Library of Medicine, 2023). The lack of a home, a roof over one’s head, really does expose a person to unsafe conditions like the ones mentioned above. It is important to be aware of these challenges to be better capable of helping those that are less fortunate. Solutions Page: There is no easy one solution to solve the problem forever, it is a nuanced issue with many different factors contributing to it. Although, beyond just hoping for governments to pass better policies, though that is also important, there are also some things you as an individual can also do. Individual Solutions: Donate: There are organizations, as well as homeless shelters and kitchens dedicated to helping these people, and donating money can contribute to continuing the work done by these organizations. Volunteer: Shelters and Kitchens also allow people to volunteer their time to help prepare meals for the homeless in these places. Keep an open mind: It is important to remember that each homeless person is a unique individual, with their own life and own challenges. Each different person may need help in a different way, and keeping this in mind is important. Institutional Solutions: While a lot can be accomplished by taking individual action, there is also more that our governments can do to help these people. Low-income support- Some causes of homelessness include poverty and lack of affordable housing (National Library of Medicine, 2023). Allocating funds to support people with low income can help financially support people in need to secure a roof over their head. Work programs- Another cause of homelessness is unemployment (National Library of Medicine, 2023). Having available resources to help these individuals get work to go on and support themselves will also help a lot of people. Mental-health support-Other causes of homelessness include mental disorders, trauma, violence or death of a loved one (National Library of Medicine, 2023). Many of these individuals face challenging mental health problems and need help and support to help empower them to improve their situations. Healthcare-illnesses, disabilities and health problems can also cause homelessness (National Library of Medicine, 2023). Improving healthcare access for these people can help uplift them. Support for substance abuse-Substance abuse is another cause for homelessness (National Library of Medicine, 2023), so having resources available for these people who struggle with substance abuse can also help with this issue. Task: Analyze Michael's commit history in Lesson 3, and then the Lesson 14 documentation, and describe what new technical concepts Michael had to learn.

Based on the provided commit history and project documentation, here is an analysis of the new technical concepts Michael had to learn when moving from the Lesson 3 project to the Lesson 14 final exam project. ### Summary of Skills from Lesson 3 Michael's work in Lesson 3 demonstrates a foundational understanding of HTML and version control. He was able to: * Create a basic HTML5 document structure (``, ``, ``, ``). * Use essential HTML tags: headings (`

`, `

`), paragraphs (`

`), and line breaks (`
`). * Add a page title (``) and multi-line comments (`<!-- -->`). * Follow a basic Git workflow: creating a file, saving, syncing, and committing with descriptive messages. This project was a single, static webpage. --- ### New Technical Concepts for Lesson 14 The Lesson 14 project, "Helping the Homeless," is a significant step up in complexity. It required Michael to learn and apply a wide range of new technical concepts to build a multi-page, styled, and interactive website. #### 1. Multi-Page Website Architecture * **Concept**: Moving from a single HTML file to a structured website with multiple interconnected pages. * **Implementation**: The project requires creating five distinct HTML pages: `homepage.html`, `policy.html`, `issues.html`, `solutions.html`, and `showsupport.html`. #### 2. Site Navigation * **Concept**: Creating a consistent navigation system to allow users to move between pages. * **Implementation**: Designing a navigation menu (likely using an unordered list of anchor tags, `<a>`) that appears on all pages. This involves using relative file paths to link to other HTML documents. #### 3. External Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) * **Concept**: Separating content (HTML) from presentation (styling). This is a core principle of modern web development. * **Implementation**: Creating an external stylesheet (`styles.css`) and linking it to every HTML page using the `<link>` tag in the `<head>`. This involves learning CSS syntax, selectors, and properties to control colors, fonts, layout, and more. The documentation specifically mentions styling a navigation menu with different colors for its default and hover states. #### 4. Advanced HTML Elements * **Forms**: Creating an interactive form on the "Show Support" page using `<form>`, `<input>` (for text, email, etc.), and buttons (`<button>` or `<input type="submit">`). * **Structured Lists**: Using different types of lists beyond basic ones. The project specifies an unordered list (`<ul>`) for issues and two description lists (`<dl>`) for solutions. * **Images**: Embedding images using the `<img>` tag with proper `src` attributes (pointing to files in an `images/` folder) and crucial `alt` attributes for accessibility. * **Metadata**: Expanding the use of metadata in the `<head>` with specific `<meta>` tags for keywords and descriptions on a per-page basis. #### 5. Responsive Design and Accessibility * **Concept**: Ensuring the website is usable on various devices (PCs, tablets, smartphones) and accessible to people with disabilities. * **Implementation**: The project documentation explicitly requires considering responsive design (making the layout adapt to screen size) and accessibility (using high-contrast colors, providing alt text for images, ensuring readable font sizes). #### 6. Client-Side Scripting (JavaScript) * **Concept**: Adding interactivity to the webpage. * **Implementation**: The project includes a reference to an external JavaScript file (`thejava.js`), indicating that Michael would need to learn the basics of JavaScript to add dynamic behavior. #### 7. Project Organization and Asset Management * **Concept**: Structuring a project with multiple files and asset types. * **Implementation**: Planning and organizing files into directories (e.g., an `images/` folder for pictures, a `css/` folder for stylesheets, a `scripts/` folder for JavaScript). The documentation includes a detailed table for tracking these assets. #### 8. Content Development and Research * **Concept**: Writing and integrating original content with proper citations. * **Implementation**: Drafting the verbiage for each page and citing external sources (like the National Library of Medicine) in APA format. ### Conclusion To complete the Lesson 14 project, Michael had to advance from building a simple, single-page HTML document to designing and implementing a full, multi-page website. The new concepts he had to learn include **multi-page architecture**, **CSS for styling**, **navigation menus**, **advanced HTML forms and lists**, **responsive design principles**, **web accessibility**, and **basic JavaScript integration**. This represents a comprehensive application of the skills taught throughout the course.
